fabricatr: what changes, what does not, and why

Source: vignettes/fabricatr2.0.Rmd
fabricatr2.0.Rmd
library(fabricatr)
set.seed(343)

The short version

fabricatr 2.0 is a ground-up rewrite of fabricatr 1.x with the same public API. Every exported function has the same name and, with a handful of exceptions catalogued below, the same signature and the same behavior. The rewrite is nine files of R against 1.0.2’s sixteen, and it is the code rather than the documentation that shrank: stripping blanks and comment lines, 1,094 lines against 1,609, while the roxygen above them grew from 751 lines to 919. Neither package has any compiled code. fabricatr 2.0 depends on dplyr, tibble, purrr, and rlang, and it does not carry 1.x’s custom workspace and evaluation machinery.

Two things motivated it. The first is speed: fabricate() sits in the innermost loop of every DeclareDesign simulation, so a constant factor there is a constant factor on every diagnosis anyone runs. The second is durability: fabricatr 1.x manages its evaluation environment with rlang machinery that rlang does not promise to keep stable, and more than once an rlang release has broken fabricatr without any change to fabricatr itself. 2.0 evaluates each column expression with a single rlang::eval_tidy() call against a plain named list, which is both the fastest and the least fragile thing available.

The headline for a collaborator porting an existing script: almost nothing changes. The rest of this vignette shows what stays the same, what moves, and why.

fabricatr 2.0 was written by its maintainers working with AI assistance (Claude, from Anthropic).

Getting it

Until 2.0 reaches CRAN, install it from the rewrite branch on GitHub and ask for the vignettes to be built:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("DeclareDesign/fabricatr@rewrite", build_vignettes = TRUE)

The branch installs under the released name, so it replaces the CRAN fabricatr in your library. To keep 1.0.2 around for comparison, install it into a separate library first and load it from there with lib.loc. Two packages of one name cannot be attached together, so restart R before switching between them.

library(fabricatr)
vignette("getting-started")   # a first tour, for someone new to the package
vignette("fabricatr2.0")      # this document

What does not change

Everything in this section is byte-identical code between the two packages, and every example below was run under both and compared row by row. All but one return the same frame from the same seed, set.seed(343), set once at the top of this page. The exception is the potential-outcomes example, whose second call starts from data: it builds the same frame from the same distribution, but lands at a different point in the random number stream, for the reason given under On reproducing an old seed.

Flat fabrication, with each column able to see the ones defined before it:

fabricate(N = 6, U = rnorm(N), X = rbinom(N, 1, 0.5), Y = U + 0.5 * X)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   ID         U     X      Y
#>   <chr>  <dbl> <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 1     -1.40      0 -1.40 
#> 2 2      0.523     0  0.523
#> 3 3      0.142     0  0.142
#> 4 4     -0.847     0 -0.847
#> 5 5     -0.412     0 -0.412
#> 6 6     -1.47      0 -1.47

Hierarchy. A second add_level() nests inside the first, exactly as in 1.x:

fabricate(
  villages = add_level(N = 3, v_income = rnorm(N)),
  citizens = add_level(N = 2, income = v_income + rnorm(N))
)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   villages v_income citizens  income
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 1           1.10  1         0.346 
#> 2 1           1.10  2         1.81  
#> 3 2          -1.60  3        -2.67  
#> 4 2          -1.60  4        -2.67  
#> 5 3           0.272 5         0.0695
#> 6 3           0.272 6        -0.0467

nest_level() is available when you would rather say so explicitly, and it does the same thing:

fabricate(
  villages = add_level(N = 3, v_income = rnorm(N)),
  citizens = nest_level(N = 2, income = v_income + rnorm(N))
)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   villages v_income citizens  income
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 1           0.273 1        -0.0101
#> 2 1           0.273 2         0.443 
#> 3 2           1.15  3         1.89  
#> 4 2           1.15  4        -0.272 
#> 5 3          -0.162 5         0.582 
#> 6 3          -0.162 6         1.92

One inherited detail is worth naming, because it looks like a contradiction until you see why it holds. The N argument of a nested level is the number of children per parent, but the N visible inside that level’s column expressions is the total number of rows the level creates. Nesting 2 citizens in each of 3 villages makes N equal to 6 inside income = v_income + rnorm(N):

fabricate(
  villages = add_level(N = 3),
  citizens = nest_level(N = 2, rows_at_this_level = N)
)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   villages citizens rows_at_this_level
#>   <chr>    <chr>                 <int>
#> 1 1        1                         6
#> 2 1        2                         6
#> 3 2        3                         6
#> 4 2        4                         6
#> 5 3        5                         6
#> 6 3        6                         6

The total is the only thing rnorm(N) can usefully draw. Were N the per-parent count, the expression would return two values, the level would have to repeat them to fill six rows, and every village would receive the identical pair of residuals. An early build of 2.0 shipped that behavior until it was caught by a regression test, and a clustered design built on it had within-cluster noise correlated at 1.00 across clusters.

A vector shorter than the level is still recycled, as in 1.x, which is what lets task = 1:3 number the tasks within every parent. Recycling is safe only because N is the total: an expression written against N already returns one value per row, so the short vectors that reach that point are the ones you wrote out deliberately. A length that does not divide the level evenly is an error.

Variable numbers of children per parent, by passing a vector:

fabricate(
  villages = add_level(N = 3, v = rnorm(N)),
  citizens = add_level(N = c(1, 2, 3), y = v + rnorm(N))
)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   villages      v citizens      y
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <chr>     <dbl>
#> 1 1        -0.787 1        -1.10 
#> 2 2         0.343 2         0.685
#> 3 2         0.343 3        -0.596
#> 4 3        -0.478 4         0.173
#> 5 3        -0.478 5        -0.449
#> 6 3        -0.478 6         0.137

Starting from data you already have:

fabricate(data = data.frame(x = 1:5), y = x ^ 2)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>       x     y
#>   <int> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1
#> 2     2     4
#> 3     3     9
#> 4     4    16
#> 5     5    25

The draw_* family, including the link-function interface:

fabricate(
  N = 5,
  x = rnorm(N),
  binary = draw_binary(latent = x, link = "logit"),
  counts = draw_count(mean = 3, N = N),
  likert = draw_likert(x, min = -3, max = 3, bins = 5),
  cat    = draw_categorical(prob = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.3), N = N)
)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   ID         x binary counts likert   cat
#>   <chr>  <dbl>  <int>  <int>  <int> <int>
#> 1 1      0.920      1      2      4     2
#> 2 2      0.118      1      2      3     2
#> 3 3     -0.624      1      2      2     3
#> 4 4     -0.179      0      3      3     1
#> 5 5      0.738      1      0      4     2

Clustered draws with a target intra-cluster correlation:

fabricate(
  clusters = add_level(N = 4),
  units    = add_level(N = 3, y = draw_normal_icc(clusters = clusters, ICC = 0.4))
)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 3
#>    clusters units       y
#>    <chr>    <chr>   <dbl>
#>  1 1        01     0.716 
#>  2 1        02     0.631 
#>  3 1        03     0.906 
#>  4 2        04     2.16  
#>  5 2        05     0.0202
#>  6 2        06     1.42  
#>  7 3        07     2.44  
#>  8 3        08     2.97  
#>  9 3        09     1.88  
#> 10 4        10    -2.24  
#> 11 4        11    -0.425 
#> 12 4        12     1.74

Potential outcomes and the switching equation. The numeric case here is unchanged; a factor or Date outcome is revealed better than it was:

po <- fabricate(N = 6, U = rnorm(N), potential_outcomes(Y ~ 0.5 * Z + U))
fabricate(data = po, Z = rbinom(N, 1, 0.5), Y = reveal_outcomes(Y ~ Z))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   ID         U  Y_Z_0    Y_Z_1     Z        Y
#>   <chr>  <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl> <int>    <dbl>
#> 1 1     -0.507 -0.507 -0.00665     1 -0.00665
#> 2 2     -0.489 -0.489  0.0111      1  0.0111 
#> 3 3      0.485  0.485  0.985       0  0.485  
#> 4 4     -1.29  -1.29  -0.793       1 -0.793  
#> 5 5     -1.78  -1.78  -1.28        0 -1.78   
#> 6 6     -1.60  -1.60  -1.10        0 -1.60

Multi-arm and factorial conditions:

fabricate(
  N = 4, U = rnorm(N),
  potential_outcomes(Y ~ 0.3 * Z1 + 0.5 * Z2 + U,
                     conditions = list(Z1 = 0:1, Z2 = 0:1))
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   ID          U Y_Z1_0_Z2_0 Y_Z1_1_Z2_0 Y_Z1_0_Z2_1 Y_Z1_1_Z2_1
#>   <chr>   <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 1     -0.0395     -0.0395       0.261       0.461       0.761
#> 2 2     -1.70       -1.70        -1.40       -1.20       -0.897
#> 3 3     -1.32       -1.32        -1.02       -0.818      -0.518
#> 4 4      0.0818      0.0818       0.382       0.582       0.882

Cluster resampling, including the ALL constant:

dat <- fabricate(
  clusters = add_level(N = 4, g = rnorm(N)),
  units    = add_level(N = 3, y = rnorm(N))
)
resample_data(dat, N = c(clusters = 2, units = 2))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   clusters      g units      y
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <chr>  <dbl>
#> 1 4        -0.264 10     0.805
#> 2 4        -0.264 10     0.805
#> 3 3        -1.54  09    -0.795
#> 4 3        -1.54  08    -1.01
resample_data(dat, N = c(clusters = ALL, units = 2))
#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#>   clusters      g units      y
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <chr>  <dbl>
#> 1 1        -0.872 03    -1.29 
#> 2 1        -0.872 03    -1.29 
#> 3 2        -1.37  06     0.918
#> 4 2        -1.37  06     0.918
#> 5 3        -1.54  07     0.922
#> 6 3        -1.54  09    -0.795
#> 7 4        -0.264 11     1.54 
#> 8 4        -0.264 12     1.80

Correlated draws through the Gaussian copula:

score  <- rnorm(200, mean = 75, sd = 10)
offers <- correlate(draw_count, mean = 3, given = score, rho = 0.6)
cor(score, offers, method = "spearman")
#> [1] 0.5212677

The realized correlation is not rho, and is not meant to be. rho is the correlation of the two normal draws underneath the copula, and the rank correlation it produces is (6/π)arcsin⁡(ρ/2)(6/\pi)\arcsin(\rho/2), which is 0.58 at rho = 0.6. A count outcome has ties, which bring that down to about 0.57, and a sample of 200 varies around 0.57 with a standard deviation of about 0.04; this one lands at 0.52. The same holds for link_levels() and for draw_normal_ar() outcomes passed through a link, below.

What changes, and why

There are twelve. Five are spellings, and a script written for 1.x still runs: each of the five old spellings is accepted and deprecated, and warns once with the call you should have written. One is a hard error, a positional N. One changes the class of what comes back, a tibble rather than a data frame. One changes the shape of the output, modify_level() named after a level above the current one. One is a deliberate fix that 1.x will not match, reveal_outcomes() keeping the type of the outcome. One changes what is drawn: total_sd is now a parameter of the distribution rather than a rescaling of the finished vector. The last two change only where in the random number stream a draw lands, which is a different kind of thing and is not a promise this package makes; see On reproducing an old seed. Each has its own section below.

One caveat on the warnings. A level constructor runs inside every simulation, so the warning fires once per call site per session rather than once per call. Under a parallel future plan the first call happens in a worker, and a warning raised there may never reach your console. So treat the table below as the authority and the warnings as a convenience, not the other way round.

fabricatr 1.0.2 fabricatr 2.0 Why
add_level(N, ..., nest = FALSE) declare_level(N, ...) Names the intent instead of negating a flag
cross_levels(by = join_using(A, B)) cross_levels(.by = c("A", "B")) Uses real dplyr::cross_join() semantics
link_levels(N, by = join_using(A, B, rho = r)) link_levels(N, .by = c("A", "B"), rho = r) Same, and rho becomes a plain argument, behind the dots
modify_level(..., by = "g") modify_level(..., .by = "g") Leading dot marks a control argument, not a column
draw_ordered(break_labels = ), draw_categorical(category_labels = ) labels = One name for the same argument across the draw_* family
fabricate(100, ...) fabricate(N = 100, ...) An error, not a warning. N is supplied by name
fabricate() returns a data.frame returns a tbl_df A different class. Same columns, same values, and identical() against a data frame is now FALSE. See below
regions = modify_level() after nesting drops the nested rows keeps them Different shape. See below
reveal_outcomes() renders a factor or Date outcome as character keeps the type A fix. 1.x lost an ordered outcome’s levels, silently. See below
total_sd rescales the finished draw total_sd is a parameter of the draw A different distribution. See below
link_levels() draws via mvnfast when installed one draw path, always Same distribution, different point in the stream, and only if you have mvnfast
fabricate(data = df, ...) burns two draws before your first column burns none Same distribution, different point in the stream

nest = FALSE becomes declare_level()

In 1.x, an independent level that will later be crossed or linked is written as add_level(..., nest = FALSE). The flag is doing real semantic work, and the name of the function actively fights it: you are not adding a level to the hierarchy, you are declaring a separate population.

It still works, and tells you what to write:

fabricate(
  countries = add_level(N = 3, gdp = runif(N), nest = FALSE)
)
#> Warning: `nest = FALSE` is deprecated in fabricatr 2.0.
#> Write:  declare_level(N = 3, gdp = runif(N))
#> Not:    add_level(N = 3, gdp = runif(N), nest = FALSE)
#> This warning is displayed once per session.
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   countries   gdp
#>   <chr>     <dbl>
#> 1 1         0.941
#> 2 2         0.794
#> 3 3         0.965

Nesting is never a flag in 2.0: a second add_level() nests, nest_level() nests, and declare_level() stands alone.

join_using() becomes .by

1.x’s join_using() is a quoting helper that exists to pass level names into cross_levels() and link_levels(). 2.0 takes a character vector instead, and performs the crossing with the same semantics as dplyr::cross_join(). join_using() is kept, and by = is accepted alongside .by =, so the 1.x spelling runs and warns.

fabricate(
  countries = declare_level(N = 3, gdp = runif(N, 1, 10)),
  years     = declare_level(N = 2, shock = runif(N, 0, 1)),
  obs       = cross_levels(.by = c("countries", "years"), Y = gdp + shock)
)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   countries   gdp years shock obs       Y
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <chr> <dbl> <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 1          8.66 1     0.853 1      9.51
#> 2 2          2.44 1     0.853 2      3.29
#> 3 3          5.37 1     0.853 3      6.22
#> 4 1          8.66 2     0.642 4      9.30
#> 5 2          2.44 2     0.642 5      3.08
#> 6 3          5.37 2     0.642 6      6.01

link_levels() samples N rows from that product rather than taking all of it, and rho is now an ordinary argument rather than something smuggled inside join_using(). The 1.x spelling, link_levels(N = 2000, by = join_using(primary, secondary, rho = 0.8)), still runs, carries its rho through, and warns with the call below:

students <- fabricate(
  primary   = declare_level(N = 20, p_quality = runif(N, 1, 10)),
  secondary = declare_level(N = 15, s_quality = runif(N, 1, 10)),
  students  = link_levels(N = 2000, .by = c("primary", "secondary"), rho = 0.8,
                          score = p_quality + s_quality + rnorm(N))
)
cor(as.numeric(students$primary), as.numeric(students$secondary),
    method = "spearman")
#> [1] 0.7685407

rho and sigma sit behind the dots in the signature, link_levels(N, .by, ..., rho = 0, sigma = NULL), so a column called r, s or si is a column and not a partial match for the correlation. The cost is that they have to be named: link_levels(N, .by, 0.5) no longer sets rho, and rho = 0.5 does.

One inherited quirk surprises people. rho is the rank correlation between the two levels’ ID assignments, not between the variables defined on those levels. Students at high-numbered primary schools are matched to high-numbered secondary schools; whether that also correlates p_quality with s_quality depends entirely on whether quality happens to rise with ID, and for a runif() draw it does not. 2.0 reproduces 1.x’s behavior here exactly, down to the same draws from the same seed when mvnfast is not installed. If you want quality-to-quality sorting, define the level variables as monotone in the level ID.

For more than two levels, pass a full correlation matrix as sigma instead of the scalar rho.

by becomes .by in modify_level()

The leading dot is the tidyverse convention for an argument that controls the verb rather than naming a column, and it removes the ambiguity that arises when a dataset happens to contain a column called by. modify_level() is otherwise dplyr::mutate(), with .by giving split-apply-combine over a grouping column:

fabricate(
  N = 12,
  cluster = rep(1:3, each = 4),
  Y = rnorm(N),
  modify_level(cluster_mean = mean(Y), .by = "cluster")
)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 4
#>    ID    cluster       Y cluster_mean
#>    <chr>   <int>   <dbl>        <dbl>
#>  1 01          1 -0.896        0.0984
#>  2 02          1  0.327        0.0984
#>  3 03          1  0.929        0.0984
#>  4 04          1  0.0338       0.0984
#>  5 05          2 -1.69        -0.238 
#>  6 06          2 -0.402       -0.238 
#>  7 07          2 -0.155       -0.238 
#>  8 08          2  1.30        -0.238 
#>  9 09          3 -1.59        -0.128 
#> 10 10          3  0.505       -0.128 
#> 11 11          3 -0.140       -0.128 
#> 12 12          3  0.713       -0.128

The old spelling groups correctly rather than quietly computing an ungrouped answer, and says what to write:

fabricate(
  N = 12, cluster = rep(1:3, each = 4), Y = rnorm(N),
  modify_level(cluster_mean = mean(Y), by = "cluster")
)
#> Warning: `by =` is deprecated in fabricatr 2.0.
#> Write:  modify_level(cluster_mean = mean(Y), .by = "cluster")
#> Not:    modify_level(cluster_mean = mean(Y), by = "cluster")
#> This warning is displayed once per session.
#> # A tibble: 12 × 4
#>    ID    cluster        Y cluster_mean
#>    <chr>   <int>    <dbl>        <dbl>
#>  1 01          1 -0.551         -0.325
#>  2 02          1  0.00535       -0.325
#>  3 03          1 -0.368         -0.325
#>  4 04          1 -0.386         -0.325
#>  5 05          2 -0.178         -0.258
#>  6 06          2 -0.728         -0.258
#>  7 07          2 -0.358         -0.258
#>  8 08          2  0.231         -0.258
#>  9 09          3  0.944         -0.498
#> 10 10          3 -1.44          -0.498
#> 11 11          3  0.273         -0.498
#> 12 12          3 -1.77          -0.498

N must be named

1.x’s signature is fabricate(..., data, N, ID_label), and a bare number in the dots, fabricate(100, Y = rnorm(N)), was read as N = 100. 2.0 does not read it that way: every expression in the dots is a column and needs a name, so the same call stops with

Every column needs a name. Expression 1 in fabricate(), `100`, has none.
  If this is the number of rows, write `N = 100`: N is supplied by name.

Write fabricate(N = 100, Y = rnorm(N)). The same rule catches an unnamed column anywhere, fabricate(N = 5, rnorm(N)), which 1.x failed on with an indexing error from deep inside and which an early build of 2.0 dropped without a word.

The result is a tibble

fabricate() returns a tibble where 1.0.2 returned a plain data frame. The columns, their order, their types, and their values are the same; only the class differs, from "data.frame" to c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"). A tibble is a data frame, so anything that takes one still works.

Two things do change for a caller. A test written expect_identical(fabricate(...), some_data_frame) compares the class attribute and now fails, which is how this surfaced: six of the eight test failures in a revdepcheck of DeclareDesign 1.1.1 are that comparison and not one of them concerns a value. And single-bracket indexing does not drop to a vector, so df[, "Y"] is a one-column tibble where 1.0.2 gave a numeric vector. df$Y and df[["Y"]] are unchanged.

modify_level() at a named level works at that level

Named after a level above the current one, modify_level() evaluates its expressions once per unit of that level: N is the number of regions, the columns in view are the ones built at the regions level or above, and each result is written back to every city in its region.

fabricate(
  regions = add_level(N = 3, a = 1:3),
  cities  = add_level(N = 2, b = rnorm(N)),
  regions = modify_level(z = rnorm(N), a2 = a * 2)
)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   regions     a cities       b       z    a2
#>   <chr>   <int> <chr>    <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 1           1 1      -0.767  -2.49       2
#> 2 1           1 2       0.516  -2.49       2
#> 3 2           2 3       0.314   0.688      4
#> 4 2           2 4       0.0860  0.688      4
#> 5 3           3 5      -1.66    0.0549     6
#> 6 3           3 6      -0.898   0.0549     6

1.x evaluates the same call the same way, three draws of z and a2 from the region’s own a, but then returns the regions frame alone: three rows, with the cities and their b gone. 2.0 keeps the six rows. An early build of 2.0 ignored the level name instead and drew one z per city, which is the silent kind of wrong, and is why this section exists.

A column built at a level nested inside is out of view at the outer level, as it is in 1.x, where the same call could see nothing below the level it named. regions = modify_level(bb = mean(b)) stops and says so, because b varies within a region. To summarise it per region, leave the level name off and group: modify_level(bb = mean(b), .by = "regions").

reveal_outcomes() keeps the type of the outcome

The one place where 2.0 deliberately declines to reproduce 1.x, because what 1.x did was wrong rather than merely different.

The switching equation picks, for each unit, the potential outcome column matching that unit’s assignment. 1.x did the picking by matrix-indexing the data frame of potential outcome columns, which goes through as.matrix(), and a matrix holds one type. So a factor outcome came back as character and a Date came back as a string. For an unordered factor that is an annoyance. For an ordered one it is a wrong answer that does not announce itself:

set.seed(1)
likert <- fabricate(
  N = 200, U = rnorm(N),
  potential_outcomes(Y ~ draw_ordered(0.6 * Z + U, breaks = c(-1, 1),
                                      labels = c("lo", "mid", "hi")))
)
revealed <- fabricate(data = likert, Z = rbinom(200, 1, 0.5),
                      Yobs = reveal_outcomes(Y ~ Z))
levels(revealed$Yobs)
#> [1] "lo"  "mid" "hi"

Those are the levels the outcome was declared with. Under 1.x, Yobs was a character vector, and the levels were gone: the natural next step, making it a factor to model it, put them back in alphabetical order as hi < lo < mid. A regression on that has the wrong baseline and, if it is treated as ordered, fits polynomial contrasts against an ordering nobody chose. Nothing warns, because nothing is malformed; the numbers are simply answers to a different question.

2.0 selects column by column instead, so the revealed vector keeps whatever the potential outcomes carried: a factor stays a factor with its levels and their order, a Date stays a Date, and numeric, integer, logical, and character are as they always were.

One case has no right answer. If the conditions disagree about their levels, there is no set to keep, and inventing an order across level sets that were never meant to be compared is worse than declining. Those reveal as character, with a warning naming the outcome and saying to give every condition the same levels.

This matters beyond fabricatr, because reveal_outcomes() is re-exported by DeclareDesign and declare_measurement(Y = reveal_outcomes(Y ~ Z)) is the idiom the book runs on. Any design with a Likert or other ordered outcome was measuring it through this.

ID columns are zero-padded character, as in 1.x

IDs are zero-padded character strings, so a design with twelve clusters gets "01" through "12" and the padding keeps character sort order matching numeric order:

fabricate(
  clusters = add_level(N = 12),
  units    = add_level(N = 2)
)
#> # A tibble: 24 × 2
#>    clusters units
#>    <chr>    <chr>
#>  1 01       01   
#>  2 01       02   
#>  3 02       03   
#>  4 02       04   
#>  5 03       05   
#>  6 03       06   
#>  7 04       07   
#>  8 04       08   
#>  9 05       09   
#> 10 05       10   
#> # ℹ 14 more rows

The type is the point. An ID is a label, not a quantity, and an integer ID is a number that R will happily use as one. lm(Y ~ clusters) on integer cluster IDs silently fits a linear trend in cluster number where you meant fixed effects, and mean(clusters) returns a value rather than an error. Character IDs make both mistakes impossible.

Note that the padding width is set per level, by the number of units at that level rather than by anything global. A frame of 4 clusters holding 3 units each carries clusters running "1" to "4" alongside units running "01" to "12", as in the ICC example above. 1.x does the same.

Levels name their own ID columns after the level, exactly as in 1.x. Flat fabrication gets a column called ID, which ID_label renames and ID_label = NA suppresses:

fabricate(N = 3, Y = rnorm(N), ID_label = "respondent")
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   respondent      Y
#>   <chr>       <dbl>
#> 1 1           0.894
#> 2 2          -1.05 
#> 3 3           1.97
fabricate(N = 3, Y = rnorm(N), ID_label = NA)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 1
#>        Y
#>    <dbl>
#> 1 -0.384
#> 2  1.65 
#> 3  1.51

total_sd is a parameter, not a rescaling

This is the one change that gives different numbers from the same call, so it gets the argument on both sides rather than an assertion.

draw_normal_icc() builds each value from a cluster-level draw and an individual-level draw, so there are four ways to describe the same pair of variances: the ICC, the within-cluster standard deviation, the between-cluster standard deviation, and the total. They are related by σtotal2=σbetween2+σwithin2\sigma_{total}^2 = \sigma_{between}^2 + \sigma_{within}^2 and ICC=σbetween2/σtotal2ICC = \sigma_{between}^2 / \sigma_{total}^2, so any two of them pin the other two.

1.x treats total_sd differently from the other three. It draws using the ICC, then rescales the finished vector so its sample standard deviation equals total_sd. 2.0 solves for the two standard deviations instead and draws once: with σtotal\sigma_{total} set by total_sd, σbetween=σtotalICC\sigma_{between} = \sigma_{total}\sqrt{ICC} and σwithin=σtotal1−ICC\sigma_{within} = \sigma_{total}\sqrt{1 - ICC}.

The consequence, over 200 draws of 100 observations with ICC = 0.4 and total_sd = 2:

mean realised sd() standard deviation of the realised sd()
fabricatr 1.0.2 2.0000 0.0000
fabricatr 2.0 1.9648 0.2225

The case for changing it. Rescaling makes the realised standard deviation exactly total_sd in every draw. A simulation that fabricates 10,000 datasets gets 10,000 datasets whose outcome variance is identical to the fourth decimal place, which no real sampling process would produce. Any diagnosand that depends on the spread of the outcome, and any standard error with an estimated variance in it, is then computed against a DGP with one of its sources of variation switched off. For a package whose entire purpose is repeated sampling, that is the wrong default. The fix also costs nothing in expressiveness, since the closed form is exact and defined at every ICC including 0 and 1.

The case against. It is a divergence, and this vignette otherwise promises that identical code gives identical results. Anyone who has calibrated a design against 1.x’s total_sd will see their numbers move. There is also a legitimate reading of total_sd under which the old behavior is correct rather than buggy: if you want a dataset whose outcome has exactly the standard deviation you named, perhaps because you are matching a published descriptive statistic, rescaling gives you that and parameterising does not. Under that reading 2.0 has taken away a feature.

Why the change anyway. The two readings are not equally served by the two implementations. If you want the parameter, you cannot recover it from the rescaled version. If you want the exact sample standard deviation, you can still have it in one line:

y <- draw_normal_icc(clusters = rep(1:10, each = 10), ICC = 0.4)
y <- (y - mean(y)) * 2 / sd(y) + mean(y)
sd(y)
#> [1] 2

One correction to the upstream discussion, because it changes what is actually at stake. The thread worries that rescaling “will possibly distort the between group differences.” It does not. Rescaling is an affine transformation and the ICC is scale-invariant, so the realised ICC is untouched; the mean R² is the same either way. The only thing rescaling changes is the sampling variability of the variance. That is a narrower objection than the thread supposes, and still a sufficient one.

A side benefit of solving rather than rescaling is that total_sd can now be paired with any of the other three. 1.x accepts total_sd only alongside ICC, because rescaling needs an ICC to draw from first. In 2.0 any two of the ICC, sd (within), sd_between, and total_sd determine the draw, so total_sd with sd_between works:

cl <- rep(1:20, each = 10)
sd(draw_normal_icc(clusters = cl, total_sd = 3, sd_between = 2))
#> [1] 3.350732

The correlated draw does not depend on your machine

link_levels(rho = ) and link_levels(sigma = ) correlate row assignments through a Gaussian copula, which needs a draw from a multivariate normal. 1.x takes that draw one of two ways:

if (requireNamespace("mvnfast")) {
  correlated_sn <- mvnfast::rmvn(N, ncores = getOption("mc.cores", 2L), mu, sigma)
} else {
  right_chol <- chol(sigma, pivot = TRUE)
  correlated_sn <- matrix(rnorm(N * ndim), nrow = N) %*% right_chol
}

The two paths consume the random number stream differently, so the same seed gives different data depending on whether an optional package is installed, and the mvnfast branch depends on your core count as well. A simulation package should not have that property, so 2.0 always takes the second path and does not suggest mvnfast at all.

The cost is nothing you can feel. mvnfast earns its name in hundreds of dimensions; link_levels() has one dimension per level, so two or three. Measured at three levels, it saves 19 milliseconds on a million rows, and nothing measurable at the sizes anyone actually links.

The consequence is that if you have mvnfast installed, a correlated link_levels() gives different numbers here than in 1.x. Without it, the two agree exactly. Either way, 2.0 gives the same numbers as itself on every machine, which 1.x cannot promise.

On reproducing an old seed

fabricatr does not promise that a given seed produces the same fabricated data in 2.0 as it did in 1.x. Two things in this release land at a different point in the random number stream than 1.x did, and neither is treated here as a break.

The reason is what the package is for. fabricatr invents data to stand in for data you do not have yet. A draw is a draw from the distribution you specified, and which particular draw you got is not a finding: re-running with a different seed is a thing you are supposed to be able to do, and a design whose conclusion depends on the seed is a design in trouble. Compare randomizr, where the draw is the result. A real assignment of real units to real treatments is a fact about the study, recorded in its data and defensible years later, so randomizr’s stream is part of its contract and does not move across versions. fabricatr’s is not, and does.

What 2.0 does promise is the part that matters: the distribution is the one the arguments describe, and 2.0 gives the same numbers as itself on every machine, which 1.x could not say, because its correlated draw ran through mvnfast when that package happened to be installed and took a core count as an argument.

So if you have a saved analysis whose numbers came out of fabricate() under a stored seed, expect them to move, and re-run and re-store rather than hunting for the difference. The two places are:

A correlated link_levels(), if you have mvnfast installed. Covered in the section above. Without that package, 1.x and 2.0 agree exactly, verified 2,000 rows deep against a library built without it.

Any call that starts from data. fabricatr 1.x calls an internal helper, makeUU(), to invent a unique name for the workspace slot it is about to put your data frame in. That helper is sprintf("%X-%X", as.integer(Sys.time()), sample.int(.Machine$integer.max, 1)), and sample.int() consumes exactly two uniforms. So every fabricate(data = df, ...) in 1.x began two draws into the stream. 2.0 has no temporary to name, because a column expression is evaluated with one rlang::eval_tidy() against a plain named list, so it starts at the beginning:

set.seed(7)
reference <- runif(6)
set.seed(7)
fabricate(data = data.frame(u = 1:6), Z = runif(6))$Z
#> [1] 0.98890930 0.39774545 0.11569778 0.06974868 0.24374939 0.79201043
reference
#> [1] 0.98890930 0.39774545 0.11569778 0.06974868 0.24374939 0.79201043

In 1.0.2 that same call returns reference[3:8]. The offset is exactly two whatever the data frame’s size, whether or not it carries an ID column, and however many columns you then build. It is pinned by a test, not because the stream position is promised, but because a silent change in it is worth knowing about deliberately rather than discovering downstream.

N is never a column

N is injected into the evaluation mask for every column expression, so rnorm(N) works everywhere it did before, but it is not written into the output. Ask for it explicitly if you want it:

fabricate(N = 3, n_obs = N, Y = rnorm(N))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   ID    n_obs      Y
#>   <chr> <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 1         3 -0.412
#> 2 2         3 -0.971
#> 3 3         3 -0.947

Beyond tidiness, keeping N out of the frame is what allows cross_levels() to work without a name collision between the two levels being crossed.

Porting an existing script

Six greps will find everything that needs to change:

# nest = FALSE          -> declare_level()
# join_using(           -> .by = c("level1", "level2"), with rho = beside it
# modify_level(... by = -> .by =
# break_labels|category_labels -> labels =
# fabricate(<number>,   -> fabricate(N = <number>,
# draw_*(prob|mean = ..., link = ) -> draw_*(latent = ..., link = )

Then run the script. You do not have to do any of it at once: the five old spellings the first four greps find still work (join_using( finds two of them), and each warns once with the corrected call, so you can port as you go and use a clean run as the signal that you are finished. The positional N is the one that stops, and its error says what to write.

Three other things stop rather than run, and each was answering the wrong question before it did. A prob or mean handed a non-identity link is refused, because the link was being dropped and the draw taken on the untransformed scale: write latent = instead, which is where a link has always acted. An N passed to draw_ordered() that is not length(x) is refused, because it never recycled x in either version. And a link name that is not one of the handful each draw accepts is refused, as it is in 1.x, rather than falling through to the identity. Nothing else needs checking: ID columns, column types, and column order all match 1.x.

What is new

Existing data frames come in as levels

import_level() makes a data frame a level of the design, which is what lets two real data sets be crossed or linked. fabricate(data = df, ...) starts from one frame and builds down from it, and that is still the way to add columns to data you already have. What it cannot do is bring in a second frame, because a level is the thing cross_levels() and link_levels() work on.

The level’s ID is the frame’s own key. A column named after the level is used as it stands, the way a join matches on a shared name, and .id names the column when it is called something else:

individuals <- data.frame(individuals = c("ann", "bob", "cyd"),
                          ind_shock = c(-0.4, 0.1, 0.8))
periods <- data.frame(year = 2020:2022, period_shock = c(0.2, -0.1, 0.3))

fabricate(
  individuals = import_level(individuals),
  period      = import_level(periods, .id = "year"),
  obs         = cross_levels(.by = c("individuals", "period"),
                             Y = ind_shock + period_shock + rnorm(N))
)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 6
#>   individuals ind_shock period period_shock obs       Y
#>   <chr>           <dbl>  <int>        <dbl> <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 ann              -0.4   2020          0.2 1     0.548
#> 2 bob               0.1   2020          0.2 2     0.183
#> 3 cyd               0.8   2020          0.2 3     1.15 
#> 4 ann              -0.4   2021         -0.1 4     1.69 
#> 5 bob               0.1   2021         -0.1 5     0.357
#> 6 cyd               0.8   2021         -0.1 6     3.42 
#> 7 ann              -0.4   2022          0.3 7     2.18 
#> 8 bob               0.1   2022          0.3 8     0.724
#> 9 cyd               0.8   2022          0.3 9     3.00

.id says which incoming column is the key. The key then takes the level’s name, so year arrives as period. Its type and values are kept, where a fabricated key is a zero-padded character string, so period still holds 2020 to 2022 and joins back to periods with by = c(period = "year"). The one column name an imported frame cannot carry is N, which is the row count in every expression a level evaluates, and which is refused rather than dropped in silence. A frame with no key of its own gets numbered rows, as add_level() numbers them. A key with a repeated or a missing value is refused, because a level’s rows are its units.

Levels nest under an imported one as they nest under any other, so a real sample of villages can carry simulated citizens:

fabricate(
  villages = import_level(data.frame(villages = c("v1", "v2"),
                                     v_income = c(10, 12))),
  citizens = nest_level(N = 3, income = v_income + rnorm(N))
)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   villages v_income citizens income
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>     <dbl>
#> 1 v1             10 1         10.5 
#> 2 v1             10 2          9.11
#> 3 v1             10 3          9.69
#> 4 v2             12 4         12.0 
#> 5 v2             12 5         13.0 
#> 6 v2             12 6         12.8

n() counts the rows in hand

n() is the number of rows the level is building, and it works in every declaration: flat, add_level(), nest_level(), cross_levels(), and modify_level(), where it counts the level being worked at. N names the same quantity and still does. The reason to have both is that N is a name: a design that also carries an N in its workspace leaves a reader unsure which one an expression reads, and redesign() rebinds names, where nothing can rebind a call. A data set that carries a column called n keeps it, because R skips non-function bindings when it looks up a call, so sum(n) reads the column and n() reads the count. 1.0.2 fails with could not find function "n".

fabricate(
  villages = add_level(N = 3, wealth = rnorm(n())),
  citizens = nest_level(N = 2, income = wealth + rnorm(n())),
  villages = modify_level(n_villages = n())
)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   villages wealth citizens income n_villages
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <chr>     <dbl>      <int>
#> 1 1         0.705 1         1.98           3
#> 2 1         0.705 2         0.890          3
#> 3 2         1.31  3         2.06           3
#> 4 2         1.31  4         1.90           3
#> 5 3        -1.39  5        -2.37           3
#> 6 3        -1.39  6        -1.66           3

Level calls and ordinary columns can be mixed in a single fabricate() call. 1.x requires that the arguments be either all level calls or none of them, so the following raises “Arguments passed to ... must either all be calls to create or modify levels, or else none of them must be”:

fabricate(
  N = 12,
  cluster = rep(1:3, each = 4),
  Y = rnorm(N),
  modify_level(cluster_sd = sd(Y), .by = "cluster")
)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 4
#>    ID    cluster       Y cluster_sd
#>    <chr>   <int>   <dbl>      <dbl>
#>  1 01          1 -0.871       0.656
#>  2 02          1  0.719       0.656
#>  3 03          1  0.111       0.656
#>  4 04          1 -0.0785      0.656
#>  5 05          2 -0.420       0.897
#>  6 06          2 -0.562       0.897
#>  7 07          2  0.998       0.897
#>  8 08          2 -1.11        0.897
#>  9 09          3 -0.142       0.811
#> 10 10          3  0.315       0.811
#> 11 11          3  1.22        0.811
#> 12 12          3 -0.699       0.811

draw_likert() accepts a manual breaks vector. The same call returns all NA under fabricatr 1.0.2:

fabricate(N = 5, x = rnorm(N), l = draw_likert(x, breaks = c(-1, 0, 1)))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   ID         x     l
#>   <chr>  <dbl> <int>
#> 1 1     -0.285     2
#> 2 2     -1.31      1
#> 3 3     -0.391     2
#> 4 4     -0.402     2
#> 5 5      1.35      4

draw_count() takes a log link, so a Poisson rate can be built from a linear predictor the way a probability is: draw_count(latent = x, link = "log") draws at exp(x). 1.0.2 refuses this outright, answering “Count data does not accept link functions”, which left no way to write a count outcome on the scale a model would fit it on. draw_binary() and draw_binomial() also accept "logistic" as a synonym for "logit", which 1.x does not.

fabricate(N = 6, x = rnorm(N), visits = draw_count(latent = x, link = "log"))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   ID           x visits
#>   <chr>    <dbl>  <int>
#> 1 1      0.591        4
#> 2 2      0.101        0
#> 3 3      0.931        4
#> 4 4     -0.263        0
#> 5 5     -0.00767      1
#> 6 6      0.367        1

draw_count() also takes dispersion, for counts that vary more than a Poisson allows, which is most counts outside a textbook. The default 0 is the Poisson draw as before, on the same random number stream. A positive value draws from the negative binomial with the same mean and variance mean + dispersion * mean^2, so dispersion = 0.5 at a mean of 3 gives a variance of 7.5 rather than 3. The parameter is Stata’s alpha and the reciprocal of the theta that MASS::glm.nb() reports, so a design can be simulated at the dispersion a fitted model found.

counts <- fabricate(
  N = 10000,
  poisson = draw_count(mean = 3, N = N),
  overdispersed = draw_count(mean = 3, N = N, dispersion = 0.5)
)
sapply(counts[c("poisson", "overdispersed")], function(y) round(c(mean = mean(y), var = var(y)), 2))
#>      poisson overdispersed
#> mean    3.01          3.01
#> var     3.02          7.59

And correlate() works with base R random number generators, not only with the draw_* family, by mapping each r* function to its q* counterpart:

x <- rnorm(200)
y <- correlate(rnorm, mean = 0, sd = 1, given = x, rho = -0.5)
cor(x, y, method = "spearman")
#> [1] -0.4719388

Panels with persistent shocks

draw_normal_ar() draws a first-order autoregressive process inside each unit of a panel: each period’s value is rho times the last one plus a fresh shock. It is the error structure behind the problem Bertrand, Duflo, and Mullainathan (2004) found in difference-in-differences, where shocks that persist within a unit make standard errors that ignore the persistence far too small, and clustering by unit repairs them. With the draw in hand, that failure can be diagnosed in a design before it happens in an analysis.

panel <- fabricate(
  units = declare_level(N = 100, unit_effect = rnorm(N)),
  periods = declare_level(N = 10),
  obs = cross_levels(
    .by = c("units", "periods"),
    e = draw_normal_ar(clusters = units, time = periods, rho = 0.8),
    Y = unit_effect + e,
    voted = draw_binary(latent = Y, link = "probit"),
    contacts = draw_count(mean = 2, quantile_y = pnorm(e))
  )
)
head(panel)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   units unit_effect periods obs        e      Y voted contacts
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>   <chr>  <dbl>  <dbl> <int>    <dbl>
#> 1 001         1.13  01      0001   0.722  1.86      1        3
#> 2 002        -1.77  01      0002   1.52  -0.249     1        4
#> 3 003         1.28  01      0003  -0.746  0.532     0        1
#> 4 004        -0.851 01      0004  -0.624 -1.48      0        1
#> 5 005        -1.96  01      0005   1.50  -0.464     0        4
#> 6 006         1.44  01      0006  -0.156  1.28      0        2

Four choices in the draw are worth knowing.

  • Each unit’s series starts at its stationary distribution, so the first period has the same variance as the tenth and there is no burn-in to discard.

  • sd is the standard deviation of the process in any one period, not of each period’s new shock. Changing rho therefore changes how persistent the shocks are and leaves the variance where it was, so designs compared across rho differ in persistence alone. stats::arima.sim() reads its sd the other way, and at rho = 0.8 the same number there gives a process 1.7 times wider.

  • The correlation between two observations of a unit is rho raised to the gap in time between them. A panel with a missing wave, or waves at uneven intervals, is the same process seen at fewer points and needs no special handling. time may be a number, a Date (read in days), or the character ID that cross_levels() gives a level.

  • The draw is a latent normal variable. A binary or count outcome with the same persistence comes from passing it on, as latent to draw_binary() or as quantile_y = pnorm(e) to draw_count(), as the example does. The serial correlation of the outcome is then weaker than rho, as it is with correlate().

The function draws persistent errors, not state dependence. A model in which this period’s outcome depends on last period’s outcome itself, a lagged dependent variable, is a different model, and fitting one with unit fixed effects in a short panel has a bias of its own.

Speed

Median time per call, measured with microbenchmark on an Apple M4 Pro under R 4.6.0, fabricatr 1.0.2, dplyr 1.2.1.

What is being built fabricatr 1.0.2 fabricatr 2.0 Speedup
Flat, N = 100, three columns 0.18 ms 0.11 ms 1.6x
Flat, N = 5,000, three columns 0.76 ms 0.57 ms 1.3x
Flat, N = 200,000, three columns 25.63 ms 22.37 ms 1.1x
Ten chained columns, N = 500 0.46 ms 0.26 ms 1.8x
Two levels, 50 villages x 20 citizens 0.56 ms 0.28 ms 2.0x
Three levels, 20 x 10 x 5 0.79 ms 0.38 ms 2.1x
Three levels, 50 x 20 x 20 (20,000 rows) 5.46 ms 2.02 ms 2.7x
Clustered draw with target ICC, 100 x 20 0.82 ms 0.42 ms 2.0x
Potential outcomes plus reveal, N = 1,000 0.71 ms 0.58 ms 1.2x

One change accounts for nearly all of it: intermediate state is a plain named list of vectors rather than a tibble, so a level that fans out 1,000 parents into 20,000 children is lapply(lst, function(v) v[idx]) instead of a tibble row-subset with its class dispatch, name repair, and validity checks. The conversion to a tibble happens exactly once, at the end. At the table’s medians, a three-level design of 20,000 rows takes 55 seconds to build 10,000 times under 1.0.2 and 20 seconds here.

The gains concentrate where design diagnosis actually spends its time, which is hierarchical data. The one row that barely moves is flat N = 200,000, where the two packages are close to parity: at that size both spend nearly all their time building the zero-padded ID strings, and 2.0 pads exactly as 1.x does. data-raw/benchmark_vignette.R re-measures every figure in this section, and in README.md, and fails when one has drifted.

Why rewrite at all

fabricatr 1.x spends most of its complexity on one question: how does a column defined early in a fabricate() call become visible to a column defined later? Its answer is a workspace, meaning a UUID-keyed environment of data frames, a pointer to the “current active df”, column expressions injected with rlang::call_modify, and dynGet("N") walking the dynamic scope to find the row count.

The tidyverse answer is a named list used as a data mask, and a loop over rlang::eval_tidy. The list being built is the mask for the next expression, so nothing has to be looked up anywhere else. No workspace, no active pointer, no dynamic scoping.

The level functions return S3 objects that fabricate() dispatches on, replacing a string-matching mode dispatcher. Hierarchy is built with plain integer indexing into lists rather than repeated data frame construction, which is where most of the speed comes from.

What survives untouched is the statistical content: draw_normal_icc(), draw_binary_icc(), correlate(), and draw_multivariate() carry real algebra with no tidyverse one-liner equivalent, and they were ported rather than rewritten.

Upstream issues

All eleven issues open on fabricatr 1.x were checked by running the reporter’s own code under both packages. Nine no longer reproduce here, and the remaining two are documentation bugs in fabricatr’s own vignettes.

The distinction in the last column is worth reading. Some of these never went wrong here, because the rewrite happened not to repeat the mistake. Others were wrong here too, and were only found because someone had already written the issue up.

Issue What it reports State here
#133 total_sd rescales the finished draw rather than being solved for jointly Fixed, and it was wrong here too. The one place a call gives different numbers than 1.x on every machine; see above
#149 draw_normal_icc() refuses ICC values at or near 0 and 1 Fixed, and it was wrong here too. Full [0, 1] range, with both endpoints treated as the degenerate cases they are
#158 draw_likert() returns a factor, ignores arbitrary breaks, and the draw_* functions share one man page Never reproduced. Integer by default, breaks honoured, ten separate man pages
#160 join() collides with dplyr Never reproduced. No such function; .by takes a character vector
#165 Data frames should be importable as levels, so two existing datasets can be crossed Fixed by import_level(), which is the one thing here that 1.x was missing rather than getting wrong. See above
#167 modify_level() before a crossed level fails with “the variable name is ambiguous” Never reproduced
#182 Variable-length hierarchy plus potential_outcomes() warns, and errors outright on R 4.2 and later Never reproduced
#188 A matrix column cannot be referenced as X.1 by a later expression Fixed, and it was wrong here too, in a different way: the matrix was kept whole, so the output had one column where 1.x had three
#189 draw_binary_icc() silently pairs the wrong probability with each cluster when prob has one value per unit Fixed, and it was wrong here too. A prob that is genuinely inconsistent within a cluster now errors instead of being quietly misread
#191 Asks for a worked copula example in the documentation Not applicable. draw_multivariate() takes the same rMvdc() formula, so the example in the issue transfers unchanged
#193 The vignettes document a type argument to draw_likert() that does not exist Not applicable. draw_likert() has bins and breaks, and these pages are new

Four of them were live defects here, found by reading someone else’s bug report rather than by testing. That is the argument for going through an upstream issue tracker after a rewrite, and not only the parts of it you expect to have inherited.

What #165 asked for. #165 wanted existing data frames importable as levels, so that a real sample of units and a real set of periods could be brought in separately and crossed. import_level() does that. The design question the prototype left open, whether an imported frame’s own key becomes the level ID or a synthetic one appears beside it, is settled in favour of the frame’s own key: a synthetic ID beside an imported one is two names for the same unit, and the imported key is the one that still matches the data it came from. See above.

Other changes worth knowing

One naming change is easy to miss. draw_ordered(), draw_likert(), and draw_categorical() all take their category names as labels. In 1.x the first is break_labels and the last is category_labels; both old names are accepted and warn once with the corrected call. The return types are 1.x’s: draw_ordered() and draw_likert() give an ordered factor, and draw_categorical() an unordered one, because its categories are nominal and an ordered factor would change which contrasts a model formula picks. Leave labels off if you want the integer codes.

Three refusals are new relative to 1.x, and all three replace a silent answer rather than a working one. A prob or mean supplied alongside a non-identity link now errors: draw_binary(prob = 0.3, link = "logit") draws at 0.3 in 1.x, where the author plainly meant plogis(0.3), and no range check can catch it, because 0.3 is a legal probability. draw_ordered() refuses an N that is not length(x), which is the one case where 2.0 stops and 1.x ran: 1.x checks N against a recycling rule it never applies, so a script relying on it was already getting length(x) back. A sigma passed to link_levels() that is not a valid correlation matrix (not positive semi-definite, an entry outside [-1, 1], the wrong dimensions, or asymmetric) now errors, as does a single negative rho across three or more levels; 1.x handed such a matrix to chol(pivot = TRUE), which warns and returns a decomposition carrying none of the requested structure. Link handling otherwise matches 1.x: an unrecognised link name errors in both, and a function passed as link is applied in both.

One difference is quieter than the rest, because it is a warning rather than a result. 1.x warns when a resampling plan names ALL for its last level, on the grounds that leaving the level out does the same thing. 2.0 accepts it silently. The frame is the same either way, and in both packages resample_data(dat, N = c(clusters = 3)) returns exactly what resample_data(dat, N = c(clusters = 3, units = ALL)) returns.

Reports of any behavior that differs from 1.x and is not listed in this vignette are the most useful thing you can send back.
